name: Oat extract
lead: Oat extract in skincare usually means colloidal oatmeal or oat kernel extracts standardized for avenanthramides, phenolic compounds in Avena sativa that are studied as an anti-inflammatory component of oats.[1] It is used in sensitive-skin, baby and sun-care products. The same name is also used for oat beta-glucan fiber extracts and green-oat extracts studied as foods or supplements, which are different preparations.[2][3][4]

Wikipedia states that the US FDA approved colloidal oatmeal as a skin protectant in 2003.[1] Oat baths were in use for itchy skin conditions in the 19th century and, according to the same source, earlier in antiquity.[1]

paras: Avenanthramides were characterized in the 1980s and have since been studied as the likely active component behind oats' soothing effect.[1] Oat kernel extracts with standardized avenanthramide levels are used in skin, hair, baby and sun-care products.[1]

The avenanthramide article proposes that these compounds may reduce inflammation by inhibiting NF-kappaB, lowering cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8, and may help interrupt the itch-scratch cycle; these are presented as hypotheses.[1] A 2008 study is reported to have found itch relief from avenanthramides comparable to hydrocortisone, though that claim is cited to non-primary sources.[1]

Published human trials of oat extracts concern oat as food or supplement rather than skin appearance: oat beta-glucan fiber extracts and blood lipids,[2] soluble oat extracts and glucose and insulin responses in moderately hypercholesterolemic adults,[3] and green-oat (Avena sativa) extract and cognitive function in middle-aged adults and during a laboratory stressor.[4][5] No studies of oat extract for skin appearance were found.

timeline.event: Colloidal oatmeal approved by the US FDA as a skin protectant, per Wikipedia.[1]

card.summary: Colloidal-oat soothing ingredient with FDA skin-protectant status; trials found for oat extracts are mostly dietary, not skin appearance.
card.note: Anti-itch and anti-inflammatory claims rest partly on non-primary sources.

quick.overview:
Oat extract in skincare is mostly colloidal oatmeal or avenanthramide-standardized extract, used to soothe dry or irritated skin.

The FDA is reported to have approved colloidal oatmeal as a skin protectant in 2003.
quick.mechanism: Avenanthramides are proposed to reduce inflammation, including through NF-kappaB inhibition, and to ease itch.
quick.risks: No safety data on cosmetic oat extract were available in the sources reviewed.
